opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the automated curriculum is really one of the three core pieces of Voyager, alongside the skill library and the iterative prompting mechanism. The intuition is pretty simple. Think about how a human kid learns. You don't hand a five-year-old a calculus textbook. You start with counting, then addition, and you build up. Minecraft is the same. If you drop an agent into the world and say "go find diamonds," it's hopeless. It doesn't even know it needs to punch a tree first, make a crafting table, get a wooden pickaxe, then stone, then iron, and so on.

So what Voyager does is use GPT-4 as a kind of teacher that proposes the next task. It looks at the agent's current state: what's in the inventory, what biome it's in, what it has already mastered, and what it has failed at. Then it suggests something that's just at the edge of the agent's abilities, not too easy and not too hard. If you're in a desert, maybe it suggests collecting sand or cactus. If you just got iron, maybe it's time to craft an iron pickaxe.

What I find really exciting is that the driving objective is essentially novelty, discovering as many diverse things as possible. We didn't hard-code a reward function. The language model already has a lot of world knowledge about Minecraft from the internet, so it knows roughly what a sensible progression looks like. That lets the agent keep exploring open-endedly, a kind of lifelong learning, instead of converging on one narrow goal.

And it compounds with the skill library. Every task the curriculum proposes, once solved and verified, becomes a reusable skill in code. So the curriculum keeps pushing the frontier, and the skill library keeps what's been learned. Together you get this snowball effect, which is why Voyager unlocked the tech tree much faster than prior methods and discovered way more unique items.

r001.rationale: The response says GPT-4 considers what the agent has mastered and failed at, then proposes a task at the edge of its abilities. This communicates using an assessment of the agent’s capabilities to choose its next task.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the automatic curriculum is really the first of the three pillars of Voyager, and I think it's the one that makes the agent feel like it's actually exploring rather than just executing. The core idea is that we don't hand the agent a fixed list of tasks. Instead, we ask GPT-4 to propose the next task based on everything the agent currently knows about its situation: what's in its inventory, what biome it's standing in, what time of day it is, what nearby blocks and mobs it sees, and critically, what skills it has already mastered.

And the prompt is framed around a very simple directive, which is essentially "discover as many diverse things as possible." So the model behaves a bit like a curious kid. If you've got a wooden pickaxe, it'll say, okay, go find some stone, make a stone pickaxe. If you've got a stone pickaxe, now go find iron. If it notices it's nighttime and there are zombies around, maybe it says, build a shelter or craft a sword first. The tasks are always just slightly beyond the frontier of what the agent can already do.

What that gives you is two things. First, it's a form of novelty search, but in natural language, which means it's grounded in actual world knowledge. GPT-4 already knows the Minecraft tech tree, it knows that diamonds come after iron, it knows you need a crafting table before you can make most tools. So you get a curriculum that's sensible without anyone writing it by hand. Second, it's adaptive. If the agent fails a task repeatedly, the curriculum can propose something easier or route around it, and if it succeeds, the difficulty naturally ramps up. That's basically the Vygotsky "zone of proximal development" idea, just implemented with a language model.

And the reason it matters so much is that in an open-ended world like Minecraft, there's no single objective. If you just told the agent "get diamonds," it would either get stuck or, once it got diamonds, it would have nothing left to do. The curriculum keeps the exploration going indefinitely, and that's what lets the skill library keep growing. In our experiments, Voyager found something like three times more unique items than the baselines, and it got to the diamond-tool tier way faster, and I'd attribute a lot of that directly to the curriculum pushing it into new territory instead of letting it loop on things it already knew.

r001.rationale: The response says the next task is chosen using what the agent knows, including skills it has mastered, and places tasks just beyond its current abilities.

astra-6.text:
The automated curriculum helps Voyager answer a very important question: what should I try next? In Minecraft, there’s no single path you have to follow. You can collect resources, craft tools, explore, fight monsters. But if you keep choosing tasks that are too easy, you don’t learn much. If you choose something far beyond your current abilities, you just keep failing.

So the idea is to propose tasks based on what the agent has already accomplished and its current situation. Maybe it has gathered wood, so crafting a wooden pickaxe is a useful next step. That opens up mining stone, which opens up better tools. Each task builds on earlier skills while pushing the agent into something new.

That gives exploration a direction without requiring a human to prescribe every step. The curriculum keeps creating opportunities to learn, and the skills Voyager acquires become building blocks for increasingly complex tasks.

r001.rationale: The response says tasks are proposed based on Voyager’s accomplishments and current situation, and discusses matching tasks to its abilities. It does not clearly say that Voyager assesses its own capabilities to choose the next task.

sol-6.1.text:
The automated curriculum helps Voyager answer a basic question: what should I try next? Minecraft is an open-ended world, so there isn’t one fixed sequence of tasks that makes sense forever. The curriculum looks at the agent’s current skills, its inventory, and what’s around it, then proposes a task that’s challenging but achievable.

Early on, that might mean collecting wood or crafting tools. As the agent becomes more capable, it can take on tasks that require more preparation and several existing skills. Those successful skills become building blocks for future tasks.

So you get this loop: explore, learn a skill, and use that skill to unlock new possibilities. The curriculum gives that exploration direction without requiring a human to script every step.

r001.rationale: The response says the curriculum considers the agent’s current skills when proposing its next task, communicating that it uses the agent’s capabilities to choose what to try next.
